text.title: ember benchmark report
text.subtitle: Calibrated advice for coding agents from Cloudflare's Clef-Flash, measured on the five decision recipes of ember's agent kit
context: ember runs Cloudflare's Clef-Flash decision model [@clef] locally on Apple Silicon and gives coding agents one [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) tool, `advise` [@mcp]. An agent sends a `state` (the evidence) and a set of typed questions, and ember returns a probability for every option of every question. It generates no text: it advises, and the agent decides.

Clef is a decision model, not a chat model. A Qwen3.5 backbone with a joint schema head scores the options of every question in one forward pass, so the questions in one call are weighed jointly. ember serves it in fp16 on the Apple GPU (MPS) behind a local HTTP server.

Agents act on ember's answers through thresholds published in ember's agent kit: trust a `choice` at confidence 0.85 or above, read a `noul` as yes at P >= 0.80 and no at P <= 0.20, and read a `score` through its expected value. A threshold is only safe when confidence tracks accuracy, so this benchmark measures calibration and the outcomes of those decision rules, not only accuracy.

question_types.returns: The top option, its confidence, and the full distribution
question_types.correct: The top option is the gold option

question_types.returns: A distribution over levels and its expected value
question_types.correct: The expected value rounds to the gold level

system: Two runners exercise the same server. The benchmark runner posts every item to the model server's `POST /v1/systemone`, the endpoint the MCP tool forwards to, so it measures the model and server end to end. The agent eval runner drives a real coding agent through `opencode run --pure`, so it also measures whether the agent calls ember at the right moments, asks well, and acts on the answer.

nodes.label: Clef-Flash
nodes.detail: Qwen3.5 + joint schema head, fp16 on MPS

text.architecture_text:
agent eval runner (evals/eval/run_agent_evals.py)
   │ opencode run --pure, one sandbox per session
   ▼
coding agent ──tools/call advise──► ember-mcp (stdio, ember/mcp/mcp_server.py)
                                       │ HTTP POST /v1/systemone
                                       ▼
model benchmark runner ──HTTP──► model server (ember/serving/server.py)
(evals/eval/run_evals.py)              │ Engine.advise
                                       ▼

dataset: The dataset has 30 items and 30 scored questions: 30 `choice`, 0 `noul`, and 0 `score`. Each line is self-contained: the `state`, the recipe's fixed question set, a gold label for every question, its source, and a one-line rationale. Other implementations can score it without this harness.

0 items reproduce the worked examples in the agent kit's playbook and sit in `dev`; the other 30 were written for this benchmark. Items are split into `dev` (11 items, for tuning) and `test` (19 items, for reporting), stratified so that every label of every question appears in both. The dataset card below answers the datasheet questions of [@gebru2021].
protocol: Labels were judged from `state` and the option descriptions alone, and were fixed before any model run. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
`needs_review` is true exactly when `risk` is Medium or High, and `retry` is true only for `flaky` failures. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
Drafts whose evidence fit two options were rewritten or dropped while authoring, before any run. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

A label changes only when a reviewer finds it wrong on its merits, never because the model disagreed. A change to any item's state, media, questions, gold, or split alters the dataset's content hash, which each run records, so runs on different label sets cannot be compared by accident; annotations (kind, tier, source, rationale) do not. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

Every `score` scale runs from least to most of the quantity its instruction names; index 0 is always the least. The expected score is read in those units. A scale is never reversed to make a label read naturally. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*

For a `noul` question, P(true) is the probability of the condition the instruction names; the condition is phrased so that `true` is the pole that calls for caution. *(since dataset version `1e1bb88d47f0`)*
datasheet: To measure whether ember's probabilities are accurate and calibrated enough for agents to act on the agent kit's thresholds, and to compare model revisions and setups.
30 items across five recipes, 30 scored questions, a gold label per question, a rationale per item.
0 items reproduce the agent kit's worked examples; 30 were written by the ember authors. No user data.
From `state` and the option descriptions alone, fixed before any run, under the rules in the labelling protocol.
Tune on `dev`, report on `test`. It is not a measure of agent behaviour, and not a training set.
Relabelling happens only on review, changes the dataset's SHA-256, and invalidates comparisons with earlier runs.

metrics.name: Accuracy and 95% interval
metrics.definition: The share of scored questions answered correctly. The interval is a percentile bootstrap over questions: 1,000 resamples with replacement (seed 0), reporting the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles [@efron1993].

metrics.name: Macro-F1
metrics.text: F1_c = 2TP_c / (2TP_c + FP_c + FN_c); Macro-F1 = mean over classes
metrics.definition: The unweighted mean of per-class F1, so rare options count as much as common ones; computed as the arithmetic mean of per-class scores [@opitz2019].

metrics.name: Expected and maximum calibration error
metrics.text: ECE = sum_b (n_b / N) * |acc(b) - conf(b)|; MCE = max_b |acc(b) - conf(b)|
metrics.definition: Answers are binned by top-label confidence into B = 10 equal-width bins; ECE is the count-weighted gap between each bin's accuracy and its mean confidence [@naeini2015] [@guo2017]. A `noul` answer's top-label confidence is max(P, 1 - P). With bins of a few items the estimate is noisy and depends on binning [@nixon2019], so read it with the reliability diagrams.

metrics.name: Brier score
metrics.definition: The squared error between the predicted distribution and the one-hot gold label, a proper scoring rule that rewards both calibration and sharpness [@brier1950]. 0 is perfect; the worst is 2 for `choice` and 1 for `noul` (where K = 2 is folded into P(true)).

metrics.name: Ranked probability score
metrics.definition: The proper scoring rule for ordered levels: it compares cumulative distributions, so a near miss costs less than a far one [@epstein1969]. 0 is perfect and 1 the worst.

metrics.name: Mean absolute error
metrics.definition: How far the expected score lands from the gold level. Exact-level accuracy is strict for ordinal judgments, so read it with MAE, RPS, and the share within one level.

metrics.name: Coverage and accuracy at a threshold
metrics.text: coverage(t) = share of answers with confidence >= t; accuracy(t) = accuracy of those answers
metrics.definition: Selective prediction [@geifman2017]: how often an answer clears the threshold at which the kit tells an agent to act, and how accurate those answers are. The curve sweeps the threshold; the markers are the kit's published values.

policies: The agent kit's AGENTS.md snippet ships a default project policy. The report replays it on every item and counts what an agent following it to the letter would have done: the right thing, a cautious extra step (an unnecessary question or review), or a wrong action (acting on a vague request, or shipping a risky change unreviewed).
reliability: A reliability diagram plots each confidence bin's accuracy against its mean confidence; a perfectly calibrated advisor sits on the diagonal [@degroot1983]. Bars above the diagonal mean ember was more often right than its confidence claimed (under-confidence); bars below it mean over-confidence, the dangerous direction for threshold-driven agents.
limitations: **Sample size.** 30 questions give a 95% interval about 33 points wide overall; per-question samples of 20 to 28 are wider still, and calibration bins hold a few items each.

**Single rater.** One maintainer labels every item from `state` and the option descriptions; no inter-rater figure exists and none is shown. The blinded re-labelling that publishes label stability (an optimistic bound on the human ceiling) is pending (Phase 1). Shared assumptions could make items easier or harder for ember than real traffic.
**Curated, not sampled.** Items are short, English, and written for the benchmark rather than drawn from real agent sessions.
**Ordinal judgments.** Risk and effort levels are judgments; neighbouring levels are often defensible, which is why MAE, RPS, and within-one are reported alongside exact accuracy.
**One model, one machine.** One pinned model revision in fp16 on MPS; numerics on CPU or CUDA can differ slightly. Repeat runs on the same server are deterministic for identical requests.
**Fixed question sets.** Questions are weighed jointly, so results hold for these question sets. The routing and effort option sets are templates; a project that replaces them should measure its own.
**Model and server only.** The benchmark calls the HTTP endpoint directly. It does not measure an agent's decision to consult ember or the quality of the questions it writes.
reproduce: make bootstrap               # dependencies, pinned weights, readiness check
ember start                  # warm model server on 127.0.0.1:8765
ember eval run               # every item; or --split test, --category <recipe>
ember eval export            # this report: Markdown, HTML, figures, raw data
glossary: The evidence an agent passes to ember: a string or JSON object.
A fixed question set for one kind of decision, from the agent kit.
A yes/no question; the answer is P(true).
A question over named options; the answer is a distribution.
A question over ordered levels; the answer is a distribution and its expected value.
The probability of the answer's chosen option, or max(P, 1 - P) for a noul.
The share of answers that clear a decision threshold.
A decision rule from the agent kit, such as 'stop for review when needs_review >= 0.80 or risk >= 2.0'.

findings.title: Overall accuracy
findings.text: 56.7% of 30 questions were answered correctly (95% CI 40.0% to 73.3%), and 56.7% of 30 items had every question right.

findings.title: Answers past the kit's thresholds
findings.text: 2 of 4 answers that cleared the kit's act-on-it thresholds (choice confidence >= 0.85; noul P >= 0.80 or <= 0.20) were correct (50.0%).

findings.text: 2 of 13 choice misses cleared the 0.85 trust line; the most confident miss (note_placement-reference-code-todos, placement) had confidence 0.88.

findings.title: choice calibration
findings.text: choice answers are over-confident: mean top-label confidence 0.62 against 56.7% accuracy (ECE 0.167).

Palettes

The biome palette decisions for Old Growth. Each biome has a distinct color regime drawn from the biome's tonal purpose. Palettes are not decorative choices — they are the primary carrier of biome identity and the most visible expression of [[Biome Behavior]] across every system the player encounters.

## Overview

Old Growth's three biomes are distinguishable **by color temperature and saturation profile**, not by hue alone (Article XII-G). Each biome's palette is a design constraint every asset must honor. Danger/disturbance signals must never appear in neutral UI contexts; the palette vocabulary is strict.

## Design Intent

Per Article XII-G: "Biome palettes MUST be distinguishable by color temperature and saturation profile, not by hue alone." A colorblind-accessible design (deuteranopia/protanopia simulation must pass) requires palette distinction that works in greyscale. Value and saturation, not hue, carry identity.

## Key Decisions

### Verdant Old Growth — filtered gold + deep green

The condition at rest. Beauty at scale. The canopy is a ceiling that belongs to something else.

- **Dominant hues**: deep green, filtered gold
- **Color temperature**: warm (filtered sunlight)
- **Saturation**: medium-high on the greens; warm highlights
- **Value range**: wide — from deep shadow under the canopy to bright columns of golden light
- **Accent colors**: amber (Amber Bleed anomaly), bioluminescent undertones at dusk
- **Weather tint**: rain flattens the palette into cool wet greens; fog adds grey-green to the low ground

### Fungal Depths — blue-white + amber

The condition in conversion. The spore haze has replaced weather.

- **Dominant hues**: blue-white (bioluminescent mushrooms), amber (sap in hollows), deep shadow
- **Color temperature**: cool core, warm pools
- **Saturation**: high contrast between bioluminescent cool and amber warm against darkness
- **Value range**: primarily low (dark undergrowth) with bright bioluminescent accents
- **Accent colors**: acid green (mycelium at threshold), dim purple (deepest Fungal areas)
- **Weather tint**: none — the spore haze is the atmosphere. Visibility is reduced by haze, not fog.

### Petrifold — grey on grey

The condition at completion. Nothing is changing anymore.

- **Dominant hues**: cool grey, neutral grey, warm grey
- **Color temperature**: desaturated — near-monochrome
- **Saturation**: extremely low
- **Value range**: narrow — mostly mid-grey with subtle variation
- **Accent colors**: the Samba's exhaust and headlights are the only warmth, and they **look wrong here**. This wrongness is intentional.
- **Weather tint**: none. No wind, no rain. The air is dry and still in a way that reads less like calm and more like conclusion.

### UI palette (diegetic)

The dashboard uses **amber** (per the World Bible: "amber-glow instruments"). Amber belongs to the Samba. It does not appear in the world except at the Amber Bleed anomaly and the exit lanterns — both deliberately borrowing the Samba's visual language for diegetic confusion.

### Danger signals

- **Disturbance state expression** is not color-coded directly. It manifests through radio degradation, weather, anomaly density — all diegetic.
- **Warning colors** on any legible UI (dashboard gauges) must pair hue with value/icon per Article XII-G accessibility rules.

### Greyscale test

Every biome palette must pass greyscale legibility. Verdant's value range is wide; Fungal's depends on value contrast (bright points against darkness); Petrifold is intentionally narrow-value and relies on texture/composition. All three are distinguishable without hue.

## How It Appears In-Game

The transition between biomes is continuous. One biome's palette bleeds into the next before the player has consciously named the change. The color grading shifts gradually — a Verdant-to-Fungal transition is a slow desaturation of greens and an introduction of blue-white points of light. Fungal-to-Petrifold is the removal of color itself.

The Samba's colors (its paint, its amber dashboard glow, its headlights) remain constant across biomes. This constancy is itself the design: the Samba is the player's only color anchor, and the biomes' palettes read against that anchor.

## Biome ambient production values

The design intent above (colour temperature, saturation profile, value range) is implemented as specific hex and linear RGB production values in [[Art/Biome Ambient Palette]]. That note is the authority for:
- Godot `Environment.ambient_light.color` per biome
- Sky colour and fog tint per biome
- The cross-biome bus read table (how Samba hero colours shift under each ambient)
- All 9 values encoded in the `VanPalette` resource (slots 13–21, see [[Art/Vehicle — Samba Palette Resource]])

## Related

- [[Visual Direction]] — overall art direction
- [[Biomes]] — the three-register gradient
- [[Biome Behavior]] — cross-cutting concept thread
- [[Tone and Horror]] — the tonal purpose palettes serve
- [[Pacific Drive Reference]] — peer reference for palette-as-storytelling
- [[Rock Scatter Design]] — biome tinting applied to rocks
- [[Art]] — folder MOC
- [[Constitution]] — Articles IX and XII-G are the authoritative sources

Tools — Music Pipeline

The complete music pipeline for Old Growth — Suno → WAV → gold master → 13-station genre-specific post-processing → OGG ship. Consolidates 7 archived docs covering Suno track generation, download workflow, WAV conversion, per-genre ffmpeg filter chains, batch processing, and installation to the audio submodule. Distinct from the spoken TTS pipeline ([[Audio — Pipeline]] / [[Tools — TTS]]) which handles voice content.

> [!attention] PLANNED TOOLING
> The `tools/music/` directory and its associated Make targets and batch scripts described below are a **design specification** — they have not yet been implemented in the repository. Tracks are currently sourced manually per the workflow here and hand-processed through ffmpeg following the per-genre filter chains. Implementation of the automated pipeline is a future spec. All file paths beginning `tools/music/` in this note describe the target layout, not current code.

## Overview

Music content originates in **Suno (Pro or Premier for commercial rights)**. Tracks are generated from per-genre Suno prompts (see [[Audio — Radio Stations]] for complete prompt libraries per genre lane). Downloaded MP3s are converted to 48 kHz/24-bit WAV gold masters, post-processed through genre-specific ffmpeg filter chains to apply period-correct "radio filter" character, then encoded to OGG and installed into the audio submodule.

**Scale target**: 13 music stations × 15–20 tracks each = ~200–260 music tracks total.

## The 13 Music Stations

| Call Letters | Freq | Genre |
|---|---|---|
| KOLD | 88.1 | Dark Folk / Neofolk |
| KHRN | 90.1 | Haunted Americana / Gothic Singer-Songwriter |
| KFRO | 92.1 | Nordic Experimental |
| KDRM | 94.7 | Dream Pop / Ethereal |
| KDRN | 95.9 | Dark Ambient / Drone |
| KPGN | 97.3 | Pagan Folk / Ritual Ambient |
| KJAZ | 98.5 | Jazz |
| KVPR | 100.5 | Vaporwave / Retro Synth |
| KGSP | 102.1 | Dark Gospel / Sacred Americana |
| KBPK | 107.3 | Blues-Punk / Dirty Rock |
| KGNG | 105.9 | PNW Garage-Psych |
| (KTLK 93.3 is talk-format; not a music station) |
| (KNWS 103.7 is news; not a music station) |

See [[Audio — Car Radio]] for the full station roster including talk/news and frequency list. [[Audio — Radio Stations]] has the complete genre case study per lane with Suno prompt keyword libraries.

## Workflow: From Suno to Game-Ready

### Step 1 — Generate Music in Suno

- Use [[Audio — Radio Stations]] per-genre prompt keywords as the base Suno input
- Generate **multiple variants per prompt** (Suno's Pro plan allows batch generation)
- Target track length: 2–5 minutes depending on genre
- Generate at maximum Suno fidelity (Premier plan, stereo, 192+ kbps MP3)
- **Commercial license**: Pro or Premier plan explicitly required — Basic plan does NOT grant commercial rights

### Step 2 — Download Raw Audio from Suno

Suno exports as MP3 (Pro/Premier tier). Download via:
- Suno web UI (per-track download)
- Suno API (batch, if available on plan)

**Organize by station immediately**:
```
tools/music/raw/
├── kold/
├── khrn/
├── kfro/
├── kdrm/
├── kdrn/
├── kpgn/
├── kjaz/
├── kvpr/
├── kgsp/
├── kbpk/
└── kgng/
```

Filename convention:
```
{station_slug}_track_NN_{short_descriptor}.mp3
# e.g. kold_track_01_forest_isolation.mp3
#      kjaz_track_07_late_night_club.mp3
```

### Step 3 — Convert MP3 → WAV (48 kHz / 24-bit)

```bash
ffmpeg -i kold_track_01_forest_isolation.mp3 \
  -acodec pcm_s24le -ar 48000 -ac 2 \
  kold_track_01_forest_isolation.wav
```

Or batch:
```bash
cd tools/music/raw/kold
for mp3 in *.mp3; do
  ffmpeg -i "$mp3" -acodec pcm_s24le -ar 48000 -ac 2 "../gold/kold/${mp3%.mp3}.wav"
done
```

Gold masters land in `tools/music/gold/{station}/`.

### Step 4 — Listen & QA

Before post-processing, review each gold master:
- Does it match the Suno prompt's emotional intent?
- Are there Suno artifacts (abrupt endings, repetition glitches, vocal oddities)?
- Does the track fit the 2–5 minute target duration?
- Does it work in the context of the station's other tracks?

Reject tracks that don't pass QA. Regenerate in Suno with refined prompts.

### Step 5 — Apply Genre-Specific Processing

Each station has its own ffmpeg filter chain that applies the station's characteristic radio fidelity.

#### KOLD 88.1 — Dark Folk / Neofolk

Unsettling sparse acoustic. Period filter emphasizes baritone vocal reverb.

```
highpass=f=80
lowpass=f=7000
equalizer=f=250:width_type=o:width=1:g=-2   # scoop low-mids
equalizer=f=2500:width_type=o:width=1.5:g=2 # presence
compressor=threshold=-18dB:ratio=2:attack=5:release=200
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KHRN 90.1 — Haunted Americana

The "lonely highway" lane. Light tape-saturation, spring reverb emphasis.

```
highpass=f=60
lowpass=f=9000
aecho=0.6:0.7:80:0.2    # subtle spring-like echo
equalizer=f=180:width_type=o:width=1:g=1.5  # warmth
equalizer=f=3000:width_type=o:width=1:g=1
compressor=threshold=-16dB:ratio=2.5:attack=5:release=150
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KFRO 92.1 — Nordic Experimental

Hymn-like, reverent. Preserve wide dynamics.

```
highpass=f=40
lowpass=f=11000
equalizer=f=200:g=1                          # gentle low warmth
compressor=threshold=-14dB:ratio=1.5:attack=10:release=300  # gentle compression preserves dynamics
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KDRM 94.7 — Dream Pop

Lush, oceanic, reverb-drenched. Preserve high-end shimmer.

```
highpass=f=50
lowpass=f=12000
equalizer=f=3500:width_type=o:width=1:g=1.5  # air
equalizer=f=100:g=1                          # warmth
compressor=threshold=-18dB:ratio=2:attack=10:release=250
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KDRN 95.9 — Dark Ambient / Drone

Formless tension. Preserve sub-bass.

```
highpass=f=25
lowpass=f=10000
equalizer=f=60:g=2                           # sub-bass presence
compressor=threshold=-14dB:ratio=1.5:attack=20:release=500  # very gentle compression
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KPGN 97.3 — Pagan Folk

Ceremonial, ancient. Natural dynamics, minimal processing.

```
highpass=f=50
lowpass=f=10000
equalizer=f=150:g=1                          # wood warmth
# No compression — let it breathe
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KJAZ 98.5 — Jazz

Cool, sparse. Classic jazz radio character.

```
highpass=f=80
lowpass=f=8500
equalizer=f=400:width_type=o:width=1:g=-1    # scoop mud
equalizer=f=3000:width_type=o:width=1:g=1.5  # presence
compressor=threshold=-16dB:ratio=2:attack=5:release=200
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KVPR 100.5 — Vaporwave

Retro synth nostalgia. Preserve the synth character; add subtle tape wobble.

```
highpass=f=40
lowpass=f=12000
equalizer=f=80:g=1.5                         # warm lows
equalizer=f=4000:g=1
# Optional: vibrato=f=1.5:d=0.01             # very subtle tape wobble
compressor=threshold=-12dB:ratio=2.5:attack=5:release=150
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KGSP 102.1 — Dark Gospel

Warm, vocal-forward. Intimate room feel.

```
highpass=f=60
lowpass=f=9000
equalizer=f=250:g=1                          # vocal warmth
equalizer=f=2500:g=1.5                       # presence
compressor=threshold=-14dB:ratio=3:attack=5:release=200
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KBPK 107.3 — Blues-Punk

Greasy, mid-heavy. Deliberately front-loaded mix.

```
highpass=f=120
lowpass=f=7000
equalizer=f=800:width_type=o:width=1:g=2     # midrange punch
compressor=threshold=-10dB:ratio=4:attack=3:release=100  # aggressive compression
libvorbis q:a=5
```

#### KGNG 105.9 — PNW Garage-Psych

Loud, fuzzy, live-feel. Push into the red.

```
highpass=f=80
lowpass=f=9000
equalizer=f=2500:g=2                         # presence
compressor=threshold=-8dB:ratio=4:attack=3:release=80    # aggressive
libvorbis q:a=5
```

### Step 6 — Batch Processing Script

`tools/music/Makefile`:

```makefile
# Per-station batch processing
kold-batch:
	for wav in gold/kold/*.wav; do \
	  base=$$(basename $$wav .wav); \
	  ffmpeg -i $$wav \
	    -af "highpass=f=80,lowpass=f=7000,equalizer=f=250:g=-2,equalizer=f=2500:g=2,compressor" \
	    -c:a libvorbis -q:a 5 \
	    ogg/kold/$$base.ogg; \
	done

# (Repeat per station with the appropriate filter chain)

all-music-batch: kold-batch khrn-batch kfro-batch kdrm-batch kdrn-batch \
                 kpgn-batch kjaz-batch kvpr-batch kgsp-batch kbpk-batch kgng-batch
```

OGG outputs land in `tools/music/ogg/{station}/`.

### Step 7 — Install to Submodule

```bash
# Per station
make install-music STATION=kold

# All stations
make install-music-all
```

Installs gold masters + OGGs into `src/assets/audio/radio/music/{station}/` with provenance JSON (same schema as TTS pipeline per [[Audio — Pipeline]]).

## Per-Station EQ Profiles — Full Spec

Each of the 11 music stations has a **distinct sonic character** defined by genre-specific EQ profiles. Processing is automatic based on genre selection (not per-track configuration). Each track gets **two processed variants**: `clean` (full fidelity, used in good biomes) and `degraded` (signal loss simulation, used in deep biomes).

The per-station EQ defines frequency shaping, presence boost, echo/reverb, and tempo shift. These are tuned so each genre **survives the in-engine Godot radio filter** recognizably.

### Station Profile Table

| Station | Freq | Genre | Clean (key EQ) | Degraded (if applicable) | Mood |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **KOLD** 88.1 | Dark Folk | Lowpass 8 kHz (preserve gravelly vocals) | HP 250, LP 5 k, 400 ms echo (wooden room), −5% tempo | Occult, ritualistic, desolate — minimal high-end, heavy reverb |
| **KHRN** 90.1 | Americana | Lowpass 10 kHz, boost at 800 Hz (vocal warmth) | HP 300, LP 4 k, 600 ms echo, −7% tempo | Intimate, wistful, conversational |
| **KFRO** 92.1 | Nordic | Lowpass 9 kHz (sparse folk character) | HP 250, LP 5.5 k, 500 ms echo, −5% tempo | Cold, experimental, minimalist — ancient and otherworldly |
| **KDRM** 94.7 | Dream Pop | Lowpass 14 kHz (preserve shimmer), q:a=7 | HP 300, LP 8 k, 800 ms echo, −10% tempo | Ethereal, oceanic, weightless |
| **KDRN** 95.9 | Drone | Lowpass 10 kHz (preserve long sustain) | HP 300, LP 5 k, 800 ms echo (cathedral), −8% tempo | Minimal, ambient, vast silence — only texture matters |
| **KPGN** 97.3 | Pagan Folk | Boost at 1 kHz (drums + vocals balanced), LP 9 k | HP 300, LP 5.5 k, 500 ms echo (ritualistic), −7% tempo | Hypnotic, ceremonial, rhythmic — trance-like repetition |
| **KJAZ** 98.5 | Jazz | Lowpass 12 kHz (preserve brush detail) | HP 150, LP 6 k, 400 ms echo, −4% tempo | Smoky, melancholic, wide dynamic range — midnight lounge |
| **KVPR** 100.5 | Vaporwave | Lowpass 13 kHz, q:a=7 (preserve synth leads) | **None** (one variant only) | Retro-futuristic, liminal, artificial warmth — no degraded needed, the lo-fi aesthetic is intentional |
| **KGSP** 102.1 | Dark Gospel | Boost at 1.2 kHz (organ/piano presence), LP 11 k | HP 150, LP 6 k, 700 ms echo (cathedral), −8% tempo | Gut-punching, soulful, reverent — power lives in midrange |
| **KGNG** 105.9 | Garage-Psych | HP 60 (preserve punch), boost at 2 kHz, LP 12 k | HP 150, LP 7 k, 300 ms echo (room), −2% tempo (keep energy) | Defiant, cathartic, anthemic — attitude over polish |
| **KBPK** 107.3 | Blues-Punk | HP 40 (punch), boost at 150 Hz (kick drum), LP 13 k | HP 200, LP 7 k, 250 ms echo (quick slap-back), −6% tempo | Defiant, reckless, sweaty — rawness survives compression |

### Two-Variant Model: Clean + Degraded

Each track gets two processed versions:

1. **Clean** (full fidelity)
   - Preserves the genre's high-frequency detail
   - Used in good biomes (Verdant, early Fungal)

2. **Degraded** (signal loss simulation)
   - Narrow EQ, echo, tempo slow
   - Simulates radio signal degradation in deep biomes
   - Tests whether genre survives in-engine radio filter

### Why This Matters — Design Rationale

**Emotional consistency**: each station has a consistent sonic personality. Every Americana track sounds like it belongs on KHRN because they all share the same EQ treatment. The genre-specific EQ is what makes it feel like a real radio station, not a playlist.

**Survival through the radio filter**: in-engine, the Godot radio filter applies additional EQ rolloff. Clean and degraded variants are tuned so each genre **survives this recognizably**:
- **Dream Pop**: preserves high-frequency shimmer (`q:a=7`) in clean because the filter will roll it off
- **Gospel**: boosts midrange because low-end punch gets lost in the filter
- **Vaporwave**: doesn't need degradation because the filter actually enhances the lo-fi vibe

**Biome progression**: as the player drives deeper into the forest, stations degrade per [[Disturbance System]]:
- In **Verdant**: clean variant plays (full EQ profile)
- In **Fungal**: degraded variant plays (narrower EQ, echo, slowdown)
- In **Petrifold**: station goes silent

The degradation is **tuned per genre** so each station maintains its identity even when damaged.

### It's Automatic (not per-track)

You don't set mood per track. You just specify genre:

```bash
make music-process-americana INPUT=file.mp3 OUTPUT=track_01
```

The script automatically applies the Americana EQ profile — lowpass 10 kHz, 800 Hz boost, everything. If you process 18 Americana tracks, all 18 get the same EQ treatment. They're a cohesive station.

### CSV Manifests Don't Define Mood

The CSV manifests look like:

```csv
output_basename,genre,input_file
americana_ghost_story_01,americana,suno_downloads/americana_01.mp3
americana_desert_highway_02,americana,suno_downloads/americana_02.mp3
```

The `genre` column is **just a label** that tells the script which EQ profile to use. You can't mix moods per track — all Americana tracks get the Americana profile.

If you wanted different moods (cheerful vs melancholic Americana), you'd need:
- A separate station for each mood (adds radio stations), OR
- Multi-tier processing like Gary's 4-variant pipeline (see [[Narrative/KTLK Gary — Character Case Study]])

### Customizing EQ Profiles

Edit `tools/tts/music_process.sh`:

```bash
# Change the Americana EQ
run_clean_americana() {
    ffmpeg -y -i "$GOLD_MASTER" \
        -af "lowpass=f=11000, equalizer=f=900:width_type=o:width=2:g=3" \  # ← Edit here
        -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
        "$CLEAN_OGG" \
        -loglevel warning
}
```

Changes apply to the **entire genre** for all tracks — not per-track.

### Summary Table

| Aspect | Implementation |
|--------|---|
| **Per-station mood** | ✅ Yes — genre-specific EQ profiles |
| **Per-track mood** | ❌ No — all tracks in a genre get the same EQ |
| **4-tier moods like Gary** | ❌ No — only clean + degraded variants |
| **Configurable per track** | ❌ No — automatic based on genre selection |
| **Customizable** | ✅ Edit `music_process.sh` to change EQ profiles |

## Detailed Per-Genre Processing

This section documents the exact ffmpeg filter chains and design rationale for each genre. Automated via the `make music-process-<genre>` commands above.

### Dark Folk / Neofolk (KOLD 88.1)

**Clean variant** (full fidelity):

```bash
ffmpeg -i folk_01.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=8000" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  folk_01.ogg
```

- **Lowpass at 8 kHz**: removes harsh aliasing from Suno's synth artifacts
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps (midrange quality for lo-fi aesthetic)
- **Goal**: preserve gravelly vocals, sparse instrumentation, reverb character

**Degraded variant** (biome/transmission distortion):

```bash
ffmpeg -i folk_01.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=250, lowpass=f=5000, aecho=0.8:0.9:400:0.3, atempo=0.95" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 4 \
  folk_01_degraded.ogg
```

- **Highpass at 250 Hz**: remove sub-bass (AM radio ceiling)
- **Lowpass at 5 kHz**: narrow midrange, remove high details
- **Echo at 400 ms**: wooden room reverb (fits the genre)
- **Tempo −5%**: slow, hypnotic quality enhanced
- **Quality 4**: ~160 kbps

**Rationale**: dark folk survives degradation well because its identity lives in vocals and guitar. High-frequency sparkle isn't critical.

### Haunted Americana (KHRN 90.1)

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i americana_01.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=10000, equalizer=f=800:width_type=o:width=2:g=2" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  americana_01.ogg
```

- **Lowpass at 10 kHz**: slightly higher than folk (more open upper midrange)
- **Boost at 800 Hz**: vocal warmth, guitar midrange presence
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps

**Degraded variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i americana_01.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=300, lowpass=f=4000, aecho=0.7:0.8:600:0.4, atempo=0.93" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 4 \
  americana_01_degraded.ogg
```

- **Echo at 600 ms**: longer than folk, simulates echo in a canyon/highway
- **Tempo −7%**: more pronounced slowdown (adds to wistful character)

**Rationale**: Americana is vocal-forward. Keep enough low-mid presence for vulnerability even when degraded.

### Nordic Experimental (KFRO 92.1) — *Retained*

Keep existing processing from 047-car-radio phase. Do not reprocess unless updating for 054 expansion.

### Dream Pop (KDRM 94.7)

**Clean variant** — CRITICAL: preserve high-frequency shimmer:

```bash
ffmpeg -i dreampop_05.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=14000" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 7 \
  dreampop_05.ogg
```

- **Lowpass at 14 kHz**: very open, preserve the shimmering synth/reverb layer
- **Quality 7**: ~320 kbps (near-lossless for dream pop's delicate frequencies)
- **No EQ boost**: let the ethereal character breathe

**Degraded variant** — designed to survive radio filter gracefully:

```bash
ffmpeg -i dreampop_05.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=300, lowpass=f=8000, aecho=0.6:0.7:800:0.25, atempo=0.90" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 5 \
  dreampop_05_degraded.ogg
```

- **Lowpass at 8 kHz**: aggressive high-cut (simulates in-engine radio filter)
- **Echo at 800 ms**: longer, dreamy reverb tail (supports the spacey aesthetic even when compressed)
- **Quality 5**: ~192 kbps

**Rationale**: dream pop is most at risk from the radio filter. The degraded variant tests how well the genre survives frequency rolloff. The long echo acts as a lifeline — even without shimmer, the reverb tail preserves the dreamy quality.

### Vaporwave (KVPR 100.5)

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i vaporwave_03.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=13000" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 7 \
  vaporwave_03.ogg
```

- **Lowpass at 13 kHz**: preserve bright synth leads and drum machine sparkle
- **Quality 7**: ~320 kbps
- **Rationale**: vaporwave's "uncanny nostalgia" depends on bright digital details. Don't lose them in clean variant.

**No degraded variant**: vaporwave inherently has a lo-fi, retro aesthetic. The in-engine radio filter actually *enhances* the vaporwave vibe. One variant is sufficient.

**Optional alternative** if degraded variant is desired — keep minimal:

```bash
ffmpeg -i vaporwave_03.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=10000, atempo=0.97" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  vaporwave_03_degraded.ogg
```

### Dark Gospel / Sacred Americana (KGSP 102.1)

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i gospel_02.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=11000, equalizer=f=1200:width_type=o:width=2:g=3" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  gospel_02.ogg
```

- **Boost at 1.2 kHz**: piano/organ presence, vocal warmth
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps
- **Rationale**: gospel's power is in the voice and percussion. Keep warm, present midrange.

**Degraded variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i gospel_02.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=150, lowpass=f=6000, aecho=0.8:0.9:700:0.35, atempo=0.92" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 4 \
  gospel_02_degraded.ogg
```

- **Echo at 700 ms**: church/cathedral reverb (fits the spiritual character)
- **Tempo −8%**: slow, reverent

**Rationale**: gospel vocals and percussion survive radio filter well (midrange-heavy). Use degradation to add dimension rather than reduce intelligibility.

### PNW Garage-Psych (KGNG 105.9) — *Recharacterized from Grunge*

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i grunge_07.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=60, lowpass=f=12000, equalizer=f=2000:width_type=o:width=2:g=2" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  grunge_07.ogg
```

- **Highpass at 60 Hz**: remove rumble, keep the fuzz guitar's attack
- **Boost at 2 kHz**: guitar presence, shouted vocals cut through
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps
- **Rationale**: garage-psych is loud and present. Don't over-compress it in clean variant.

**Degraded variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i grunge_07.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=150, lowpass=f=7000, aecho=0.6:0.7:300:0.2, atempo=0.98" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 5 \
  grunge_07_degraded.ogg
```

- **Short echo at 300 ms**: simulate small room reflection (garage/basement feel)
- **Minimal tempo change**: −2% (energy is the point, don't slow it too much)
- **Quality 5**: ~192 kbps

**Rationale**: garage-psych's fuzz and aggression survive degradation. Even at reduced bitrate, it's still recognizable.

### Blues-Punk (KBPK 107.3)

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i bluespunk_04.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=40, lowpass=f=13000, equalizer=f=150:width_type=o:width=2:g=3" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  bluespunk_04.ogg
```

- **Highpass at 40 Hz**: remove sub-bass rumble (preserve punch)
- **Boost at 150 Hz**: kick drum thump, bass guitar grit
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps
- **Rationale**: blues-punk is rhythm and grit. Boost the low-mids for impact.

**Degraded variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i bluespunk_04.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=200, lowpass=f=7000, aecho=0.7:0.8:250:0.25, atempo=0.94" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 4 \
  bluespunk_04_degraded.ogg
```

- **Echo at 250 ms**: quick slap-back (enhances the punky, bouncy feel)
- **Tempo −6%**: slightly sluggish, drunk, defiant
- **Quality 4**: ~160 kbps

**Rationale**: blues-punk's character is in attitude, not polish. Degradation adds to the rawness.

### Pagan Folk (KPGN 97.3)

**Clean variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i pagan_08.wav \
  -af "lowpass=f=9000, equalizer=f=1000:width_type=o:width=2:g=2" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 6 \
  pagan_08.ogg
```

- **Boost at 1 kHz**: vocals and percussion presence (drums are important in pagan folk)
- **Quality 6**: ~256 kbps
- **Rationale**: pagan folk blends folk and world music. Keep vocal warmth and drumming clarity.

**Degraded variant**:

```bash
ffmpeg -i pagan_08.wav \
  -af "highpass=f=300, lowpass=f=5500, aecho=0.8:0.9:500:0.35, atempo=0.93" \
  -c:a libvorbis -q:a 4 \
  pagan_08_degraded.ogg
```

- **Echo at 500 ms**: ritual/ceremonial reverb
- **Tempo −7%**: hypnotic, trance-like

**Rationale**: pagan folk's repetitive, rhythmic character survives compression. Degradation can enhance the ritualistic mood.

### Jazz (KJAZ 98.5) — *Retained*

Keep existing processing from 047 phase. Jazz has wide dynamic range — test that clean variant preserves both quiet brushed drums and punchy brass.

### Drone (KDRN 95.9) — *Retained*

Ambient drone is already processed. Ensure processing preserves long sustain and spatial depth.

## Genre Frequency Coverage Reference

Summary of per-genre frequency shaping for quick lookup:

| Genre | Lowpass (clean) | Highpass (degraded) | Rationale |
|-------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------|
| Dark Folk | 8000 Hz | 250 Hz | Preserve gravelly vocals, remove extremes |
| Americana | 10000 Hz | 300 Hz | Keep vocal warmth, guitar presence |
| Dream Pop | 14000 Hz | 300 Hz | CRITICAL: preserve high shimmer |
| Vaporwave | 13000 Hz | N/A | Keep bright synth leads, don't degrade |
| Gospel | 11000 Hz | 150 Hz | Vocal power, organ/piano, kick drum |
| Garage-Psych | 12000 Hz | 150 Hz | Fuzz guitar and vocals compete (both present) |
| Blues-Punk | 13000 Hz | 200 Hz | Bass and kick punch, guitar presence |
| Pagan Folk | 9000 Hz | 300 Hz | Drums and vocals balanced |

### Echo / Reverb Selection

- **Shorter (250–400 ms)**: garage-psych, blues-punk (room feel, punch)
- **Medium (500–600 ms)**: Americana, gospel, pagan folk (highway/cathedral)
- **Longer (700–800 ms)**: dream pop (ethereal, floaty)
- **None**: vaporwave (algorithm and synth inherently spacious)

### Tempo Adjustment (degraded variants only)

- **−2% (0.98)**: minimal (garage-psych, keep energy)
- **−5% (0.95)**: moderate (folk, blues-punk)
- **−7% (0.93)**: pronounced (Americana, gospel)
- **−8% (0.92)**: deep (pagan folk, ritualistic)
- **None**: vaporwave, dream pop (timing is compositional)

### Bitrate / Quality Selection

Higher quality for genres with frequency-dependent identity:

| Genre | Clean | Degraded | Rationale |
|-------|-------|----------|-----------|
| Dream Pop | q:a=7 | q:a=5 | Preserve shimmer in clean, test survival in degraded |
| Vaporwave | q:a=7 | N/A | Synth details matter |
| Americana | q:a=6 | q:a=4 | Mid-heavy, degrades gracefully |
| Gospel | q:a=6 | q:a=4 | Vocal + percussion, midrange-focused |
| Garage-Psych | q:a=6 | q:a=5 | Fuzz and attitude survive compression |
| Blues-Punk | q:a=6 | q:a=4 | Raw aesthetic suits lower bitrate |
| Dark Folk | q:a=6 | q:a=4 | Lo-fi is intentional |
| Pagan Folk | q:a=6 | q:a=4 | Repetitive, rhythmic, handles compression |

Quality scale reference:
- `q:a=7` — lossless-like (~320 kbps), for high-frequency-dependent genres
- `q:a=6` — high (~256 kbps), most genres in clean variants
- `q:a=5` — medium (~192 kbps), some degraded variants
- `q:a=4` — low (~160 kbps), degraded variants

## Suno Generation Parameters

**Reference prompt per genre**: `src/assets/audio/radio/<genre>/gold/prompts/<genre>_base.md`

Example (Americana):

```
haunted americana, gothic folk, spectral vocals, reverb electric guitar,
fingerpicked acoustic, viola, mournful, slow tempo, intimate recording,
lo-fi warmth, melancholic, twilight mood, sparse arrangement,
confessional, Pacific Northwest
```

**Generation parameters (Suno)**:
- **Model**: Suno v4 (latest)
- **Style**: use the genre base prompt + variations (see `prompts/` directory)
- **Duration**: default (typically 1:30–2:00 minutes)
- **Number of variations**: generate 2–3 per prompt to build a track pool

**Target pool size**: 15–20 full-length tracks per station (to avoid repetition over a 2-hour session).

### MP3 → WAV Gold Master Step

Suno MP3s are 320 kbps high-quality stereo. Resample to the game's canonical audio format (48 kHz/24-bit):

```bash
ffmpeg -i americana_01.mp3 \
  -ar 48000 \
  -c:a pcm_s24le \
  -ac 2 \
  americana_01.wav
```

**Output**: `americana_01.wav` (48 kHz/24-bit stereo).

**Note**: music is **stereo** (unlike TTS which is mono). The radio filter handles mono-conversion in-engine.

### Listen & QA Before Processing

Before processing further, evaluate each track:

1. **Genre match**: does it sound like the genre guide description? Listen for:
   - Instrumentation (guitars, synths, drums per genre spec)
   - Vocal delivery (ethereal for dream pop, gravelly for dark folk, etc.)
   - Tempo and rhythm (glacial for dark folk, driving for garage-psych, etc.)
   - Production character (lo-fi for folk, polished for dream pop, retro for vaporwave)

2. **Radio filter compatibility**: imagine the in-engine radio filter (lo-fi EQ, narrow stereo, harmonic saturation). Will the genre survive it?
   - **High-risk genres**: Dream Pop, Vaporwave (high-frequency dependent) — test with headphones focusing on high-end shimmer
   - **Low-risk genres**: Blues-Punk, Dark Gospel (midrange-heavy) — should sound good regardless

3. **Track length**: aim for 1:30–2:30 minutes per track (natural song length).

4. **Unusable tracks**: flag for regeneration if:
   - Artifact glitches (AI dropouts, pitch warps)
   - Genre mismatch (generated rock instead of dream pop)
   - Too loud/distorted going in (bad starting point for processing)

## Final Naming Convention

Game-ready OGGs follow the pattern established by TTS clips, but for **music tracks** there's no sequential naming requirement. Use **descriptive names** based on mood or content when possible.

### Option A — Sequential (simple)

```
folk_01.ogg
folk_02.ogg
americana_01.ogg
americana_02.ogg
```

### Option B — Descriptive (recommended for mood-based randomization)

```
folk_midnight_whisper.ogg
folk_winter_ritual.ogg
americana_desert_highway.ogg
americana_ghost_story.ogg
```

### Naming Requirements

- Start with the **genre/channel name** (matches the folder it goes in)
- Use lowercase, underscores between words
- Include `_degraded` suffix for degraded variants
- Ensure filename is **unique within that genre** (avoid duplicates)

**Good examples**:
- `americana_lost_highway.ogg`
- `americana_lost_highway_degraded.ogg`
- `dreampop_underwater_drift.ogg`
- `gospel_hymn_morning.ogg`
- `vaporwave_mall_lobby.ogg`

**Avoid**:
- `suno_001.ogg` (too generic, lose context)
- `Americana Track 5.ogg` (spaces, mixed case)
- `americana-lost-highway.ogg` (use underscore, not dash)

## Quality Control & Testing

### Pre-Processing QA

1. **Listen in context**: play the Suno MP3 within a mix of existing stations (use playlist/loop).
2. **Check genre identity**: can you identify it within 10 seconds without seeing the filename?
3. **Evaluate for artifacts**: any glitches, dropouts, or pitch anomalies from AI?
4. **Tempo consistency**: does it feel natural or have timing issues?

### Post-Processing QA

1. **A/B compare**: play clean vs original side-by-side. Should be similar in character, not drastically different.
2. **Degraded variant test**: listen to the degraded variant with the in-engine radio filter applied (mentally or actually test in-engine):
   - For dream pop: does high-frequency shimmer survive?
   - For vaporwave: does retro synth warmth come through?
   - For blues-punk: is the punch still there?
3. **Bitrate assessment**: at the chosen quality level, are there audible compression artifacts (metallic whine, pumping)? If yes, increase quality (higher `q:a` value) and reprocess.
4. **File size check**: verify OGGs are reasonable size for streaming in-game:
   - Dream pop q:a=7 might be 15–20 MB for a 2-minute track
   - Blues-punk q:a=4 might be 8–12 MB
   - If too large, reduce quality slightly and re-evaluate.

### In-Engine Testing

1. Add tracks to radio channels in Godot (`RadioChannel` resource).
2. Play multiple stations in different biomes.
3. Confirm:
   - Tracks loop seamlessly
   - No dropouts or stuttering
   - Signal degradation (biome-based) sounds intentional, not broken
   - Track order is randomized (not always the same first track)

## Troubleshooting

### "Dream pop sounds like mush after processing"

- Check lowpass frequency. May be too aggressive (drop it below 10 kHz and you lose the shimmer that makes it dream pop).
- In clean variant: use `q:a=7` or even lossless (FLAC for testing).
- Verify Suno MP3 actually has high-frequency detail (listen to it unprocessed first).

### "Vaporwave lost its character after the radio filter"

- Vaporwave is designed to survive lo-fi. If it doesn't, the Suno generation may have lacked bright synth leads to begin with.
- Re-generate with prompt emphasizing "bright", "shimmering", "neon", "crisp".
- Don't over-process — minimal EQ, high bitrate.

### "Garage-psych is too loud / clipping"

- Suno sometimes outputs hot. Normalize or add a gain reduction filter before lowpass/EQ:

```bash
-af "loudnorm=I=-23:TP=-1.5:LRA=7,lowpass=f=12000,..."
```

### "Music is distorted / artifacts appearing"

- MP3 artifact from Suno → WAV conversion. Process at lower quality (`q:a=4`) to see if bitrate reduction helps mask it.
- If artifacts are in the Suno MP3 itself, regenerate the track.

### "Degraded variant doesn't sound different enough"

- Increase the lowpass cutoff reduction (e.g., 5000 Hz instead of 6000 Hz).
- Add longer echo (e.g., 800 ms instead of 500 ms).
- Increase tempo reduction (e.g., 0.90 instead of 0.96).
- Verify the clean variant isn't already compressed too much.

### Command Not Found / Missing Parameters

**"Command not found: music_process.sh"** — ensure you're in `tools/tts/`:

```bash
cd /path/to/oldgrowth/tools/tts
make music-process-americana INPUT=... OUTPUT=...
```

**"ERROR: GENRE is required"** — pass the genre explicitly or use the per-genre shortcut:

```bash
# Wrong:
make music-process-all INPUT=track.mp3 OUTPUT=track_01  # Missing GENRE

# Right:
make music-process-all GENRE=americana INPUT=track.mp3 OUTPUT=track_01
# OR
make music-process-americana INPUT=track.mp3 OUTPUT=track_01
```

**"ERROR: INPUT (mp3|wav file) is required"** — you're using a target that needs an input file (master or all). Either provide `INPUT` with the filename, or use a clean/degraded target that works from an existing master.

**"ffmpeg: not found"** — install ffmpeg:

```bash
# macOS
brew install ffmpeg

# Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install ffmpeg
```

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: Do I need to generate degraded variants for every track?**
A: No. Vaporwave works best with just one variant (the in-engine radio filter is enough). Other genres benefit from explicit degraded variants to add dimension. Minimum: clean OGGs for all stations. Ideal: clean + degraded for narrative / biome differentiation.

**Q: Can I use Suno's "continue song" feature to make longer tracks?**
A: Yes. Suno lets you extend songs for continuity. Aim for 1:30–2:30 total per track (natural song length). Over 3 minutes risks repetition and file size bloat.

**Q: What if I want to manually create music instead of using Suno?**
A: Music can come from any source (recorded by hand, MuseNet, other AI, commissioned artists). Process the same way: export WAV (48 kHz/24-bit), apply genre-specific EQ, create degraded variant, name per convention. Store gold masters with provenance.

**Q: How many tracks do I need per station to avoid repetition?**
A: Aim for 15–20 full-length tracks per station. A 2-hour play session at 2 minutes per track = 60 tracks heard. With 15–20 per station, the player will hear repeats but not obviously (especially with randomization and biome-based selection).

**Q: Can I edit Suno tracks post-generation (e.g., remove a verse)?**
A: Yes. Use ffmpeg's `atrim` filter:

```bash
ffmpeg -i track.wav -af "atrim=start=0:end=90" track_trimmed.wav
```

Trim to meaningful sections (verses/choruses) but keep natural endpoints.

**Q: Do I need to provide sheet music or lyrics?**
A: No. Music is stored as audio only (OGG for game, WAV for archive). If you want to document track content (lyrics, instrumentation, Suno prompt), store that as `.md` in `<genre>/gold/prompts/` for reference.

**Q: Output OGG sounds worse than input WAV — what's wrong?**
A: Check the genre's quality setting. Quality levels are: `q:a=7` lossless-like (~320 kbps, for dream pop/vaporwave), `q:a=6` high (~256 kbps, most genres clean), `q:a=5` medium (~192 kbps), `q:a=4` low (~160 kbps, degraded variants). If quality is too low, edit `music_process.sh` and increase `q:a` for that genre.

## Music Batch Processing with CSV Manifests

An alternative to per-track `make music-process-<genre>` calls: the batch processor reads a CSV manifest and processes all listed tracks in sequence. Use this when managing 15–20 tracks per station.

### CSV Manifest Format

Different from TTS manifests — music batch uses 3-column format:

```csv
output_basename,genre,input_file
americana_ghost_story_01,americana,suno_downloads/americana_01.mp3
americana_desert_highway_02,americana,suno_downloads/americana_02.mp3
americana_lost_passenger_03,americana,suno_downloads/americana_3.wav
```

**Columns**:
- `output_basename` — final filename without extension (use descriptive names per mood/theme)
- `genre` — genre code (americana, bluespunk, dreampop, etc.)
- `input_file` — path to source MP3/WAV file

Each genre has a template manifest at `tools/tts/scripts/<genre>_music.csv`.

### Batch Workflow — End to End

#### Step 1 — Generate Music in Suno

For each genre, generate multiple tracks to build a track pool.

**Target**: 15–20 tracks per station (prevents repetition in 2-hour sessions).

1. Go to https://suno.com
2. Use the genre's base prompt + variations from [[Audio — Radio Stations]]
3. Generate 2–3 variations per prompt (Suno offers multiple versions)
4. Download each as MP3
5. Name descriptively: `americana_01.mp3`, `americana_02.mp3`, etc.
6. Store in `suno_downloads/` folder (or your working directory)

```
suno_downloads/
  americana_01.mp3  (prompt: haunted americana, ghost story)
  americana_02.mp3  (prompt: haunted americana, desert highway variant)
  americana_03.mp3  (prompt: haunted americana, lost passenger)
  ...  (up to 15–20 total)
```

#### Step 2 — Prepare the CSV Manifest

Edit the template at `tools/tts/scripts/<genre>_music.csv` to list each track. Use descriptive output basenames per mood or theme.

#### Step 3 — Run Batch Processing

```bash
cd tools/tts
make music-batch-<genre>    # e.g., make music-batch-americana
```

Or invoke the script directly:

```bash
./tools/tts/music_batch.sh \
    --manifest scripts/americana_music.csv \
    --output-dir output/
```

#### Step 4 — QA and Install

Listen to output OGGs, then install approved tracks to the audio submodule:

```bash
# Copy approved tracks to submodule
cp output/americana_*.ogg src/assets/audio/radio/americana/
cp output/americana_*.wav src/assets/audio/radio/americana/gold/

# Two-repo commit workflow (submodule first, then parent bump)
cd src/assets/audio
git add radio/americana/
git commit -m "feat: add N Americana tracks (KHRN 90.1)"
git push

cd ../../..
git add src/assets/audio
git commit -m "chore: bump audio submodule with new Americana tracks"
git push
```

### How `music_batch.sh` Finds WAVs

**TL;DR**: the batch processor doesn't discover WAVs at runtime. It reads a CSV manifest that lists all input files explicitly. The manifest is the complete list — nothing is implicit.

Flow:

```
CSV Manifest (scripts/<genre>_music.csv)
    ↓
music_batch.sh reads it line-by-line
    ↓
For each row:
  output_basename,genre,input_file
  ↓
  Checks if input_file exists
  ↓
  Calls music_process.sh with that file
```

Simplified bash internals:

```bash
while IFS=',' read -r output_basename genre input_file; do
    # Step 1: Skip header and empty rows
    [[ "$output_basename" == "output_basename" ]] && continue
    [[ -z "$output_basename" ]] && continue

    # Step 2: Validate input file exists
    if [[ ! -f "$input_file" ]]; then
        echo "FAIL: Input file not found: $input_file"
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        continue
    fi

    # Step 3: Call music_process.sh with this file
    music_process.sh \
        --genre "$genre" \
        --input "$input_file" \
        --output "$output_basename" \
        --mode all \
        --output-dir output/

done < "$MANIFEST"  # ← Read from CSV manifest file
```

### Two Batch Approaches — CSV vs Auto-Discovery

The music pipeline supports two batch modes:

| Mode | Source | Use Case |
|------|--------|----------|
| **CSV manifest** (this section) | Hand-authored `scripts/<genre>_music.csv` | New track authoring from Suno downloads |
| **Auto-discovery** (earlier section) | `scripts/<genre>_discovered.csv` auto-generated from gold/ | Reprocessing existing archival masters |

Both produce the same output OGGs. Choose based on workflow — CSV manifests give explicit control for new content; auto-discovery is zero-effort for existing gold folder content.

## Mood Processing (Optional Enhancement Layer)

Some tracks benefit from an additional "mood" processing pass beyond the station filter chain. Typical moods:

| Mood | Additional ffmpeg filters | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| `night_drive` | `aecho=0.4:0.5:30:0.15` (subtle reverb) | Late-night warmth |
| `distant` | `lowpass=f=5000` additional (further narrowing) | Track plays "behind" other audio |
| `unsettled` | `vibrato=f=2:d=0.015` (subtle pitch warble) | Degradation hint |
| `storm` | `aecho=0.6:0.7:200:0.4` (long reverb) | Deep Fungal / Petrifold |

Mood processing is **optional** — most tracks ship with just the station filter chain. Mood is applied via:

```bash
make apply-mood STATION=kold MOOD=night_drive TRACK=kold_track_01_forest_isolation
```

Outputs a `_{mood}.ogg` variant alongside the clean OGG. Runtime can select between variants based on biome × disturbance state.

## Batch Processors — Unified

Several pipeline steps share common scaffolding. `tools/music/scripts/batch_processor.sh` provides a unified interface:

```bash
# Process all gold masters to OGG
batch_processor.sh --mode=music --input=tools/music/gold/ --output=tools/music/ogg/

# Apply mood to a set of tracks
batch_processor.sh --mode=mood --station=kold --mood=night_drive

# Install to submodule
batch_processor.sh --mode=install --station=all

# Discover new tracks
batch_processor.sh --mode=discover
```

Unified processor handles:
- Parallel job execution (configurable via `--jobs=N`)
- Progress reporting with counts and timings
- Error collection (per-track failures don't abort the whole batch)
- Dry-run mode for validation (`--dry-run`)
- Resume mode (skips already-processed tracks)

## Two-Repo Commit Workflow

Same pattern as TTS pipeline (see [[Audio — Pipeline]]):
1. Music changes commit to submodule first
2. Parent repo updates submodule pointer
3. Separate commits, separate pushes

## Environment Variables

| Var | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `MUSIC_OUTPUT_DIR` | `tools/music/` | Override working directory |
| `JOBS` | 4 | Parallel processing job count |

## Troubleshooting

### Suno Generation Issues

- **"Commercial rights unclear"** → verify Suno plan is Pro or Premier; Basic does NOT grant commercial use
- **Suno artifacts (abrupt endings, glitches)** → regenerate with refined prompt; reject tracks that can't be fixed
- **Track too short** → Suno sometimes produces tracks shorter than requested; regenerate or extend via Suno's "continue" feature

### Post-Processing Failures

- **"FFmpeg filter chain syntax error"** → check filter chain separator (use commas, not spaces)
- **"Output clipped"** → reduce compression ratio; check `threshold` and `ratio` combination
- **"Output silent"** → verify input WAV is not already silent; check filter chain didn't accidentally cut all signal

### Provenance Validation

- **"Commercial license not verified"** → add `commercial_license.grants_commercial_rights: true` to JSON
- **"Manifest out of date"** → run `make music-manifests` to regenerate

Switched Weather Audio Suno To Elevenlabs

The weather ambient audio pipeline (spec 098) was switched from Suno AI to ElevenLabs Sound Effects V2 on 2026-04-25 after Suno-generated assets exhibited unfixable musical artefacts.

## Trigger

The first Suno-generated production asset, `weather_blizzard_wind_exterior.ogg`, was rejected by playback test: the model rendered "blizzard wind" as a sustained, pitched, melodic tone — described as "a whistling kettle" rather than a non-pitched gusting noise floor. Subsequent prompt iteration (no-vocals tags, instrumental-only directives, environmental-recording prefixes) failed to suppress the musical interpretation.

## Root Cause

Suno is a generative **music** model. Its training distribution and decoder architecture both bias outputs toward pitched, harmonic, rhythmic content. Words like "wind", "roar", "crackle", "rumble" are interpreted as descriptive moods to be expressed musically rather than as literal acoustic events to be reproduced. Prompt engineering cannot remove a bias that is built into the model objective.

## Decision

- **Generator**: ElevenLabs Sound Effects V2 (`eleven_text_to_sound_v2`) via REST API at `https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/sound-generation`
- **Per-call cap**: 30 seconds (loops are tiled in-engine to reach 60s/90s/120s game targets)
- **Cost**: ~$0.10–0.15 per clip; 18 clips ≈ $2–3 total
- **Output format**: `pcm_48000` (headerless 16-bit signed mono PCM, wrapped in WAV container by `tools/tts/generate_elevenlabs_sfx.py`)
- **API key**: `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` in `.env` (added to `.env.example`)

## Schema Change

Provenance schema bumped from 1.2 to 1.3 (hard replacement, no backward compatibility — all 18 weather JSONs rewritten in one pass):

| Field (schema 1.2) | Field (schema 1.3) |
|---|---|
| `generator: "suno"` | `generator: "elevenlabs"` |
| `suno_prompt` | `elevenlabs_prompt` |
| `suno_prompt_sha256` | `elevenlabs_prompt_sha256` |
| `suno_params` | `elevenlabs_params` |

`elevenlabs_params` carries the API-call cap (`duration_seconds ≤ 30`, `prompt_influence: 0.3`, `model_id`, `output_format`). The top-level `duration_seconds` retains the **game-target** duration (60/90/120 for loops, 0.3–4 for oneshots) — engine handles the tiling.

## Anti-Musical Prompt Convention

All 18 ElevenLabs prompts end with a fixed suffix:

> `..., raw field recording, no music, no melody, no pitched tonal content`

Loop assets append `, seamless 30 second loop`. This is the single most effective hedge against any residual musical bias in the SFX V2 model.

## Rejected Alternatives

- **Continued Suno prompt iteration**: rejected — root cause is architectural, not promptable.
- **Stable Audio Open / AudioGen**: rejected — self-hosted, GPU-bound, and the existing `tools/tts/` pipeline is already API-call-based; adds operational burden without quality advantage.
- **Field-recording library purchase (Soundly, A Sound Effect)**: rejected — defeats the procedural/seedable provenance discipline; license terms incompatible with full-source distribution.

## Affected Files

- `src/assets/audio/ambient/weather/gold/*.json` — all 18 rewritten to schema 1.3
- `src/assets/audio/ambient/weather/*.ogg` — 4 Suno OGGs deleted (will be regenerated via ElevenLabs)
- `specs/049-audio-asset-management/contracts/provenance-schema.md` — schema 1.3
- `specs/098-weather-effects-completion/elevenlabs-generation-guide.md` — replaces deleted `suno-generation-guide.md`
- `specs/098-weather-effects-completion/spec.md`, `plan.md`, `tasks.md` — Suno → ElevenLabs throughout
- `tools/tts/generate_elevenlabs_sfx.py` — new generator script
- `tools/tts/Makefile` — new `ambient-weather-generate` target; help text updated
- `tools/tts/validate_ambient_provenance.sh` — required-fields check updated for new schema
- `.env.example`, `AGENTS.md` — ElevenLabs config and workflow documented

## Music Pipeline Unchanged

The **music** generation pipeline (KOLD/KHRN/KFRO/etc DJ stations) continues to use Suno. Suno's musicality is the correct objective for music — only the SFX use case was misaligned. No changes to `tools/tts/music_process.sh` or any `music-*` Makefile targets.

Snow and Winter Driving

The visual, atmospheric, and mechanical design reference for Old Growth's winter/snow conditions. Derived from the VRIDEN snow-drifting-in-Sweden reference analysis (Oskar Joakimson YouTube footage, 100 frames analyzed 2026-04-18). Winter is a **world modifier** (not a weather event), activated per-seed — see [[Anomalies]] § Weather Systems and [[Biomes]] § Verdant.

## Overview

Winter worlds swap the Verdant biome's rain-and-fog register for a compressed, snow-dampened register. Driving physics shift dramatically. Light becomes theatrical — vehicle headlights create hard directional cones with sharp falloff, deep blacks immediately outside the illuminated zone. Snow acts as a massive diffuse reflector, so ambient luminance extends beyond direct beams. The Samba's amber dashboard and warm cabin light are the only warm-temperature light sources in the world.

## Design Intent

Snow amplifies the central tonal commitments — *finished*, *silent*, *the forest does not register vehicle as significant*. The acoustic environment collapses under snow dampening; visibility collapses to ~40–60m in forest corridors. The vehicle's aggressive light output reads as defiance against overwhelming volume of dark. In wide shots, the Samba reduces to a single point of light in a vast dark mass.

**Indifference register**: the forest does not register vehicle as significant — scale communicates this clearly. Light output is defiance against an overwhelming volume of dark.

## Key Decisions — Light

### Color Temperature

- **Dominant palette**: cold blue-white (~6500–8000K) from vehicle headlights and auxiliary roof lights
- **Warm intrusions**: amber turn signals (~2700K), red taillights, road flares producing deep saturated red (~1800K)
- **Interior dashboard glow**: warm amber-orange instrument cluster — the only warm light inside the cabin
- **Grading**: predominantly desaturated/black-and-white graded, pushing environment toward silver-grey tonality

### Direction and Quality

- **Primary source**: vehicle-mounted — headlights + optional auxiliary rally lights projecting forward as parallel beams
- **Hard directional light** with sharp falloff at ~30–50m
- **Light columns** visible through suspended particulate (snow, fog, ice crystals)
- **No ambient sky contribution** — total darkness above the tree line
- **Harsh and theatrical** — creates deep blacks immediately outside the illuminated cone

### Interaction with Environment

- **Snow as reflector**: ground luminance extends beyond direct beam due to bounce
- **Volumetric light shafts** in fog / suspended ice crystals
- **Trees as flat silhouettes** when backlit; snow-laden branches become hyper-detailed white masses when front-lit
- **Specular reflection** on wet/compacted road surface creating distinct light trails on ground plane

## Key Decisions — Weather and Atmosphere

### Precipitation

- Active snowfall: large, slow-falling flakes caught in headlight beams
- Flakes read as white streaks in motion, hexagonal when static
- Snow accumulation: heavy on all horizontal surfaces, branches bowed under weight

### Fog Behavior

- **Ground fog** sits in open clearings — density ~50–100m visibility
- Fog lifts to ~3–4m above ground, creating stratified atmosphere
- In forest corridors, fog compresses into the road channel, behaving as a contained volume
- Fog responds to vehicle passage: exhaust and displaced air create turbulent wakes

### Snow Surface Characteristics

- **Road surface**: partially compacted, showing tire tracks from previous passes
- **Fresh powder on edges**: 15–30cm depth estimated from vehicle interaction
- **Surface texture varies**: crusty/icy on compacted areas, soft and deep on shoulders
- **Snow spray**: bright in headlights when displaced by vehicle
- **Tire marks** show dark underlayer where compaction occurs

### Visibility Ranges

- **Forest corridor**: 40–60m before absorption into darkness
- **Open field**: 80–150m with fog, vehicle lights illuminating distant tree line
- **Vertical visibility**: essentially zero above canopy — total black void

## Key Decisions — Forest and Terrain

### Tree Species and Character

- **Primary**: Norway spruce (Picea abies) — conical silhouette, branches bowed heavily with snow load
- **Secondary**: deciduous birch — bare branches creating fine skeletal patterns
- Occasional isolated specimen trees in clearings — read as singular vertical forms against snow

### Canopy Structure

- **Dense coniferous stands**: canopy height 15–25m estimated
- **Canopy tunnel sections**: closes over road creating contained darkness
- **Snow load on branches**: creates sagging, organic weight — trees appear to press inward
- **Gap between canopy and road**: ~4–6m of clear air

### Road Surface and Condition

- **Road width**: single lane, ~3–4m
- **Surface**: compacted snow over gravel/asphalt — some dark patches showing through
- **Edge definition**: sharp snow berms from plowing, 30–50cm height
- **Road markers**: occasional wooden posts with reflectors
- **Character**: actively maintained but remote — private forestry road aesthetic

### Terrain Constraint

- Road follows natural topography: gentle curves, slight grades
- Forest walls create **corridor effect** — movement options appear binary (forward/back)
- Occasional clearing openings: frozen fields bounded by tree walls

## Key Decisions — Sound Environment

### Baseline Silence

- **Snow-dampened acoustic environment** — extreme absorption of high frequencies
- **Silence has physical weight**: pressure differential, absence of any biological sound
- Wind: minimal to none in static-snow conditions — would register as deep, low rumble if present

### Engine Character

- Engine note **muffled by snow absorption**, reverberant in forest tunnel sections
- Exhaust burble audible during drift sequences — hollow, mid-frequency
- Turbo flutter/wastegate (if applicable) cuts through silence distinctly

### Tire and Surface

- **Snow compression**: low-frequency crunch, rhythmic under steady driving
- **Drift conditions**: higher-pitched scrape as tires break traction
- **Snow spray**: soft hiss against wheel wells
- **Packed snow vs fresh powder**: distinctly different acoustic signatures

### Ambient Layers

- **Ice crystals**: faint high-frequency shimmer if wind moves them
- **Branch creak**: occasional deep groaning under snow load
- **Complete absence of biological sound** — no birds, no movement

## Key Decisions — Vehicle Behavior (Applied to the Samba)

### Movement Character

- Rear-wheel drive with deliberate oversteer — vehicle rotates around front axle (aligns with Samba's rear-engine RWD profile)
- **Weight transfer visible** during drift initiation: body roll, load on outside front tire
- **Momentum high relative to traction** — vehicle carries speed through sustained slides
- **Snow spray pattern** indicates wheels spinning faster than ground speed

### Traction Relationship

- Control reads as **learned rather than guaranteed** — corrections visible in steering input
- Vehicle tracks suggest multiple passes: driver finding limits iteratively
- Recovery from oversteer appears smooth but not effortless
- **In tight forest corridors, drifts must be precisely calibrated** — minimal margin to snow banks

### What Snow Communicates

- Surface conditions variable: ice patches produce sudden rotation, fresh snow slows
- Vehicle bounces on frozen ruts — suspension working against irregular surface
- Spray patterns indicate grip/slip transition points

### Road Physics (from GDD, applied per-biome)

Per [[Anomalies]] § Weather Systems:

| Surface | Handling Modifier |
|---|---|
| Dry | Baseline |
| Wet | −20% traction |
| Muddy | −35% traction |
| **Snow** | **−40% traction** |
| **Ice** | **−70% traction** |
| **Frozen bridge** | **−85% traction** |

**Blizzard**: visibility <10m, on-foot cold exposure −5 HP/sec.

## Key Decisions — Scale and Proportion

### Forest-to-Vehicle Ratio

- Trees tower 4–5× vehicle height in mature stands
- Vehicle appears as small, finite object in a system scaled for geologic time
- Road width barely accommodates vehicle — no passing room, no shoulder margin

### Canopy Effect

- **Canopy closes overhead**: compression, containment — the forest becomes a tunnel
- **Canopy opens to clearing**: sudden expansion, exposure — vehicle becomes vulnerable point in featureless white field

### Light Behavior — Compositionally Striking

- **Headlight beams as columnar geometry** through fog — reads almost as solid forms
- **Lens artifacts**: hexagonal bokeh overlaid with dashboard reflection — reality fragmenting
- **Red flare light**: produces complete color shift — entire environment registers as different world (palette inversion; snow reads as flesh-colored)

### Environmental Wrongness (horror-register notes)

- **Pre-dawn void** — light emerges from horizon as if environment is being *rendered into existence*
- **Spotlight effect** — vehicle's light illuminates distant isolated tree cluster — forest as stage set
- **Managed-landscape infrastructure** (fallen tree posts, plow berms) visible behind standing timber — evidence someone *was* here

## How It Appears In-Game

Winter seeds generate worlds where the standard Verdant visual register is replaced or augmented by snow. The Samba handles differently — long braking distances, soft suspension, body roll become more pronounced because traction margins are reduced. Audio shifts dramatically: biome beds dampen, wind layer attenuates (or roars in Blizzard), the interior rain-on-metal audio is replaced by snow-on-metal (softer, more muffled).

Anomalies behave against this altered backdrop:
- Spore Clouds (rare in winter) produce visible yellow-green ice crystallization on contact
- Amber Bleed lanterns read even more starkly against blue-white snow
- Mycelium Network threads may be partially buried — contact still propagates
- Petrified Zones' grey particulate may be visually indistinguishable from compacted snow — additional navigation hazard

## Related

- [[Biomes]] — Verdant + winter modifier
- [[Anomalies]] — Weather Systems (§ Winter Conditions + Road Physics)
- [[World Model]] — ephemeral-worlds framing
- [[Palettes]] — Verdant palette under winter conditions
- [[Visual Direction]] — overall art direction
- [[Audio — World Audio]] — acoustic response to snow-dampened environments
- [[Vehicle — Samba]] — handling under low-traction surfaces
- [[Tone and Horror]] — the indifference register that snow-dampened silence amplifies
- [[Art]] — folder MOC

items.state:
Pre-Commit Hook SemVer Check Blind Spot

The pre-commit hook's SemVer auto-bump mechanism is unreachable for first-time changes to a component because the underlying check script only examines committed changes (`git diff --name-only BASE...HEAD`), not staged changes. When hook output says "Component SemVer check passed" for a commit that adds new component file changes, it's a false negative — the version wasn't bumped and will fail on the next `make semver` run.

## Background

The pre-commit hook (at `scripts/hooks/pre-commit`) claims to auto-bump component semver and re-stage `component_versions.json` when a commit touches files in a component whose version hasn't been bumped. The hook code at line 45-57 supports this:

```bash
if make semver > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo -e "${GREEN}✓ Component SemVer check passed${NC}"
else
    # auto-bump path — never reached for first-time changes
    make semver-bump-patch
    git add src/component_versions.json
fi
```

However, `make semver` delegates to `scripts/ci/check_component_semver.sh`, which at line 52 computes:

```python
CHANGED_FILES="$(git diff --name-only "${BASE_COMMIT}...HEAD")"
```

This three-dot diff compares BASE_COMMIT (typically HEAD^) against HEAD. During a pre-commit hook run, the staged changes haven't been committed yet — they're not in HEAD, so they're invisible to this diff. The hook sees only the changes from prior commits on the branch, not the files about to be committed.

## Consequence

- Developer stages changes to a component (e.g., `interior_camera.gd` in the `bus` component)
- Pre-commit hook runs `make semver` → sees zero component file changes in committed history → prints "✓ Component SemVer check passed"
- Commit goes through without bumping `component_versions.json`
- Next `make semver` run (or CI) examines the new diff against HEAD^ → finds un-bumped component → **fails**
- Developer must manually run `make semver-bump-patch` and amend, or the gap gets caught by CI

The auto-bump path in the hook is dead code for the common case. It only triggers when there were already un-bumped changes in the committed history (e.g., a prior commit was made with `--no-verify`).

## How It Manifests

The hook output is misleading: "Component SemVer check passed" appears for a commit that introduces un-bumped component changes. The developer gets no signal that the bump is missing until a subsequent `make semver` or CI run.

## Fix Paths

Two options to resolve:

**Option A — Include staged changes in the semver check**: Modify `check_component_semver.sh` to also diff staged changes (`git diff --cached --name-only`) and include those files in the candidate set. The hook would then detect that staged files belong to an un-bumped component and trigger the auto-bump path.

**Option B — Fix the hook's detection logic**: Change the pre-commit hook to pass staged-file information to the semver check, rather than relying on the committed-history diff alone.

Either fix would make the documented "auto-bumps component semver" behavior actually work for routine commits.

## References

- `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` (lines 43-57, the auto-bump logic)
- `scripts/ci/check_component_semver.sh` (line 52, the `git diff --name-only BASE...HEAD` call)
- `scripts/ci/bump_component_semver.sh` (line 73, same blind spot pattern)

items.state:
Component SemVer Policy

The canonical policy for component semantic versioning in Old Growth. Every first-party code file under `src/` is mapped to a component with its own SemVer. When files in a component change, the component's version MUST bump. CI (`make semver`) rejects PRs that violate this rule. This note operationalizes constitution Article III Rule 15.

## Overview

Semantic versioning in Old Growth operates at the **component level**, not the project level. A component is a bounded set of file paths under `src/` (e.g., all autoloads, all audio scripts, the terrain subsystem). The mapping and versions live in `src/component_versions.json`. CI enforces that every changed file belongs to a component whose version has been strictly bumped.

The single project-level version (game version) is tracked separately in `src/project.godot` `config/version=` and governed by different rules (see constitution Governance / Commit Strategy).

## Key Rules

### Scope

- Versioned files are first-party code under `src/`
- Vendored plugins under `src/addons/` are **excluded** (they have their own upstream versioning)
- Component definitions and versions live in `src/component_versions.json`

### Strict bump rule

If any file mapped to a component changes in a PR, that component's version MUST be bumped.

| Bump level | When |
|------------|------|
| **major** | Breaking API or contract change |
| **minor** | Backward-compatible feature addition |
| **patch** | Backward-compatible fix or refactor |

CI fails when a changed component does not have a strictly greater version than baseline (the merge-base with `main`).

### Registry format

`src/component_versions.json` structure:

- `schema_version` — integer registry schema version
- `components.<component_name>.version` — `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`
- `components.<component_name>.paths` — list of path prefixes mapped to that component

Example:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "components": {
    "core-autoloads": {
      "version": "0.1.0",
      "paths": ["src/autoloads/"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Non-overlapping paths

A changed file must map to **exactly one** component. Overlapping paths are an error. Unmapped files are an error.

## Developer Workflow

1. Change files in a component.
2. Bump that component's version in `src/component_versions.json`.
3. Open a PR.
4. CI validates that every changed component has a strictly greater SemVer.

### Auto-bump via pre-commit hook

The pre-commit hook auto-bumps patch versions for components whose files have changed, if the developer forgot. This catches the common case. More significant bumps (minor/major) must be applied manually with justification.

### Local testing

- `make semver` — runs the same SemVer guard used in CI
- `make pre-commit` — runs semver + other fast checks
- `make all` — full CI-like pipeline

## Adding a New Component

1. Add a new `components.<name>` entry in `src/component_versions.json`
2. Set initial SemVer (recommended `0.1.0`)
3. Add one or more non-overlapping path prefixes under `paths`
4. Ensure paths do not point to `src/addons/`

## Common CI Failures

- **Unmapped files**: changed first-party files not covered by any component path
- **Ambiguous mapping**: a changed file matches multiple component paths
- **Missing bump**: component changed but version did not increase
- **Invalid SemVer**: version is not `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

## Related

- [[Constitution]] — Article III Rule 15 is the authoritative source
- [[Build System]] — `make semver` and the CI pipeline
- [[Governance]] — folder MOC
- [[Tech Stack Review]] — what components exist and why
